## Where We're Headed

*From planning what to build, to the design patterns that make it feel effortless.*

1. **Designing effective processes** — prioritizing requests, assembling a team, mapping the flow
2. **Dialogue management patterns** — happy paths, fallbacks, clarification loops, graceful degradation
3. **Case studies** — how Alexa, Google Assistant, and enterprise chatbots actually handle this
4. **Patterns meet principles** — connecting dialogue design to accessibility and calm technology

## Designing Effective Processes {background-color="#BA0C2F"}

::: {.kicker}
PART ONE
:::

*A conversational AI is a complete user experience channel — its design sets the ceiling on how good it can be.*

## What the User Sees — and What They Don't

*An original diagram of Freed's core design principle: invisible parts still need to work well.*

```{mermaid}
%%{init: {'theme':'base', 'themeVariables': {'primaryColor':'#BA0C2F','primaryTextColor':'#fff','primaryBorderColor':'#7A0A22','lineColor':'#C0AC7E'}}}%%
flowchart TD
    V["VISIBLE: 'Set an alarm for 9 p.m.' →
    'I've set an alarm for 9 p.m.'"]
    V --> I1["1. Utterance sent to NLU"]
    I1 --> I2["2. Intent + entity returned"]
    I2 --> I3["3. Matching response found"]
    I3 --> I4["4. Orchestrator calls the API"]
    style V fill:#BA0C2F,color:#fff
    style I1 fill:#FAF8F5,color:#333
    style I2 fill:#FAF8F5,color:#333
    style I3 fill:#FAF8F5,color:#333
    style I4 fill:#FAF8F5,color:#333
```

::: {.callout}
Freed's point: the user experiences only what they say and what you say back. Everything in between must still be designed carefully for that experience to feel good.
:::

## Don't Boil the Ocean {background-color="#003B5C"}

*An impossibly large scope is the fastest way to stall a conversational AI project.*

::: {.callout}
Freed's advice: brainstorm everything your assistant could conceivably do, then build an iterative plan instead of trying to launch it all at once. High-frequency, low-complexity requests should always come first.
:::

**Where the data comes from:** review call logs, search queries, and interview subject-matter experts. Shadow your call center staff for a day if you have one. The closer you are to real user data — and the farther you are from opinions — the better this exercise works.

## The Volume × Complexity Grid

*An original recreation of Freed's Fictitious Inc. prioritization exercise.*

| | Lower complexity | Higher complexity |
|---|---|---|
| **Higher volume** | Store hours & location, Get contact info | Open account, Reset password, Schedule appointment |
| **Lower volume** | Apply for a job, Check loyalty status | Report fraud, Transfer points |

*Table 3.1's Customer Care intents, sorted into Freed's grid: quick wins (top-left), bigger investments (top-right), nice-to-haves (bottom-left), and rarely-worth-it (bottom-right).*

## A Generalized Plan: Focus, FAQ, or Escalate {background-color="#BA0C2F"}

*The same grid, turned into an actual decision rule for what to build.*

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.tag-cardinal}
**Focus** (high volume, low complexity)

Fully automate as many of these as you can — the highest ROI in the whole grid.
:::

::: {.tag-cardinal}
**FAQ or Escalate** (high volume, high complexity)

Decide: quick-win answer, or route to a human-staffed channel?
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**FAQ, as time permits** (low volume, low complexity)

Worth addressing eventually — don't over-invest here.

**Escalate** (low volume, high complexity)

May never be worth automating.
:::
:::

## Assembling Your Dream Team

*Production-grade conversational AI needs more than one person's expertise.*

| Role | What they bring |
|---|---|
| **Business-Process SME** | Understands the business and its current, as-is processes in depth |
| **UX Designer** | Advocates for the user, making sure the conversation delivers what users want |
| **Developer / Technical SME** | Codes the dialogue rules and confirms what's technically possible |
| **Legal** | Makes sure legal and regulatory concerns are addressed before launch |
| **Marketing** | Keeps the assistant's tone and content aligned with the brand |
| **Project Sponsor** | "I'm making sure we deliver a coherent solution." |

*Freed, A. (2021). Conversational AI. Manning Publications, Ch. 3.*

## Mapping a Process Flow: Password Reset {background-color="#003B5C"}

*An original recreation of Freed's labeled process-flow convention — easier to say "P04" than "the node after we ask for date of birth."*

```{mermaid}
%%{init: {'theme':'base', 'themeVariables': {'primaryColor':'#BA0C2F','primaryTextColor':'#fff','primaryBorderColor':'#7A0A22','lineColor':'#C0AC7E'}}}%%
flowchart LR
    P00["P00: Reset
    password request"] --> P01["P01: Ask
    for user ID"]
    P01 --> P02["P02: Known?
    Look up user"]
    P02 --> P03["P03: Ask
    date of birth"]
    P01 --> P04["P04: Match?"]
    P04 --> P05["P05: Ask
    security question"]
    P05 --> P06["P06: Match?"]
    P05 --> P07["P07: Reset
    password"]
    P06 --> P08["P08: Cannot
    reset password"]
    P03 --> P09["P09: Intent
    closure"]
    style P00 fill:#BA0C2F,color:#fff
    style P07 fill:#8A2A0E,color:#fff
    style P08 fill:#7A0A22,color:#fff
```

*Reset only happens after both checks pass. Any failed match routes to P08, never to a reset.*

## Choosing Your Channel: Voice vs. Web

*The channel you pick shapes nearly every later design decision.*

| | Web | Voice |
|---|---|---|
| **Technical complexity** | Fewer moving parts; no speech training needed | Adds speech-to-text and text-to-speech |
| **Reach** | Requires a website, app, or browser | Ubiquitous — almost everyone has a phone |
| **Output richness** | Text, images, buttons, links | Text readout only — no visuals |
| **Input certainty** | You know exactly what was typed/clicked | You get a transcription, which can be wrong |
| **Best for** | Users already comfortable online | Non-tech-savvy users, hands-busy situations |

## Dialogue Management Patterns {background-color="#003B5C"}

::: {.kicker}
PART TWO
:::

*What separates good conversational AI design from bad? Four recurring patterns, grounded in real design practice.*

## What Separates Good Design from Bad?

*A 1995 essay on ubiquitous computing offers a surprisingly durable answer.*

::: {.callout}
Writing in Computer-Mediated Communication Magazine, Xerox PARC researcher Mark Weiser argued that the most profound technologies are those that disappear — that force people to adapt their whole lives to the machine, instead of blending naturally into it.
:::

**Applied to conversational AI:** bad design constantly reminds you that you're talking to a machine — rigid menus, brittle phrasing requirements, dead ends. Good design lets the conversation feel natural even when things go wrong.

*Weiser, M. (1995). The Technologist's Responsibilities and Social Change. CMC Magazine, 2(4).*

## The Happy Path: Design's Starting Point {background-color="#BA0C2F"}

*The sequence you designed for — but voice users rarely stay on it.*

::: {.callout}
Amazon's own developer team defines the happy path as the sequence you expect most customers to follow. In voice, defining the happy path is only the starting point — what defines a good voice experience is how well it handles customers who veer off it.
:::

**A concrete example:** your happy path offers three sizes: small, medium, large. A customer asks for something your menu never anticipated — "gigantic," or "how big is large?" That moment is where design either forces the customer back into a rigid script, or handles the detour gracefully.

## When Users Leave the Happy Path

*Two responses to the same off-script moment — one loses the user, one keeps them.*

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.tag-cardinal}
**The rigid response**

"Please say small, medium, or large." The customer is forced to learn your interface's rules instead of being understood.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**The adaptive response**

"Large is about the size of a refrigerator — are you thinking more medium or large?" The system rolls with the customer's direction.
:::
:::

*Amazon Developer Blog. Why Voice Design Matters: We Don't Speak the Way We Write.*

## Pattern 1 · Fallbacks

*A safety net for input the system was never trained to expect.*

::: {.callout}
A fallback catches whatever doesn't match any trained intent, and gives the system something reasonable to say instead of silence or a raw error.
:::

**Fallbacks are not failures:** Google's own developer guidance treats fallback handling as core design work — every turn needs one, because off-script input can happen at any point.

**A good fallback still moves the conversation forward:** rather than a dead-end "I don't understand," offer a next step — rephrase, try an example, or reach a human.

## Google's Error Taxonomy {background-color="#7A0A22"}

*Google's official conversation design guidance names three distinct kinds of failure.*

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.tag-cardinal}
**No Input**

The system heard nothing — the user was silent, distracted, or the microphone closed with no response.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.tag-cardinal}
**No Match**

The system heard something, but couldn't interpret it in the current context.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.tag-cardinal}
**System Error**

A backend system the assistant depends on can't complete the task.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.callout}
Google's guidance is explicit: with good error handling, the user won't even know an error occurred at all.
:::

*Google for Developers. Conversation Design: Errors.*

## Pattern 2 · Clarification Loops

*Not every ambiguous input needs a fallback — sometimes it just needs a good follow-up question.*

::: {.callout}
A clarification loop asks a targeted follow-up when the system is close but not certain — rather than giving up and falling back.
:::

**Google's design principle: assume cooperation.** Official guidance instructs designers to assume the user is being cooperative, even when it's unclear — the system's job is to figure out what the user meant, not to make the user guess the system's rules. Context matters too: the second or third attempt should sound different from the first.

## How Many Reprompts? {background-color="#BA0C2F"}

*Three independent sources converge on the same answer: not many.*

| Source | Limit | What it covers |
|---|---|---|
| **Google Assistant** | 3 | No Input / No Match errors in a row before exiting |
| **Google Assistant (collection)** | 2 | No Match attempts to collect one piece of information |
| **Freed's two-strikes rule** | 2 | Consecutive low-confidence guesses before escalating |

*The common thread: every additional attempt costs user patience. Once two or three attempts fail, the user stops trusting the system entirely.*

## Pattern 3 · Graceful Degradation

*When the ideal response isn't available, offer the best one that still is.*

::: {.callout}
Graceful degradation means a system keeps providing real value even as conditions get worse, instead of failing outright. Google's guidance is direct: end the conversation gracefully when there's genuinely nothing you can do to help, rather than stalling the user with vague promises.
:::

**What it looks like in practice:** redirecting Report Fraud requests straight to a human hotline (Freed's Fictitious Inc. example) is graceful degradation in action — the assistant recognizes its limits and hands off cleanly.

## Graceful Degradation Meets Accessibility {background-color="#003B5C"}

*The W3C's Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) formalize the same idea at web scale.*

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="25%"}
::: {.tag-cardinal}
**Perceivable**

Presentable to users in ways they can perceive.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="25%"}
::: {.tag-cardinal}
**Operable**

Usable by everyone, regardless of how they interact.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="25%"}
::: {.tag-cardinal}
**Understandable**

Information and operation must be understandable.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="25%"}
::: {.tag-cardinal}
**Robust**

Works reliably across current and future assistive tech.
:::
:::
:::

*Robustness, in WCAG's sense, is graceful degradation by another name. W3C WAI. WCAG 2 Overview.*

## Anatomy of a Good vs. Bad Error Message

*The same underlying failure, handled two very different ways.*

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.tag-cardinal}
**A bad example**

"Sorry, I can't hear that." Implies the user simply spoke too quietly — users often respond by raising their voice, which doesn't fix a system issue.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**A good example**

"Sorry, I can't sell this product right now. Please visit our website." Names the real limitation honestly and gives a concrete next step.
:::
:::

## These Patterns Play Out Differently by Channel {background-color="#7A0A22"}

*The same pattern, implemented very differently depending on whether users can see it.*

| | Web | Voice |
|---|---|---|
| **Fallback** | A visible message, plus suggested buttons | A brief spoken apology — nothing to visually scan |
| **Clarification** | Can show multiple options at once | Must ask one question at a time, kept short |
| **Graceful degradation** | Can link out to a website for more detail | Must fully resolve or clearly redirect |

## The Cost of a Long Greeting

*Freed's own timed comparison shows how quickly good design becomes bad design.*

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.tag-cardinal}
**20 seconds**

to the first useful piece of information. A typical automated phone greeting buries its one useful instruction at the very end — 62 words, 20 seconds of audio.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**4 seconds**

to the same point, rewritten. "Thanks for calling So-and-So. Calls are recorded. How can I help you?" covers the same basics far faster.
:::
:::

*Freed cites Pascal's famous observation that it takes real editing work to write briefly — "I have not had the time to make it shorter," as Pascal himself once put it.*

## Case Studies {background-color="#BA0C2F"}

::: {.kicker}
PART THREE
:::

*How Alexa, Google Assistant, and enterprise chatbots put these patterns into practice.*

## Case Study · Amazon Alexa's Happy-Path Philosophy

*A skill ecosystem built around designing well for the moments off the happy path.*

::: {.callout}
Amazon's own developer guidance frames voice's biggest design challenge directly: users don't speak the way they write, and won't stay inside your defined happy path. A skill's quality, in Amazon's own words, is revealed by how well it lets customers take the lead when they veer off it.
:::

**The design lesson:** a skill that only handles "small, medium, large" verbatim will frustrate users the moment they say anything else — which, in voice, happens constantly.

## Case Study · Google Assistant's Error-Handling Rules {background-color="#003B5C"}

*The most formally specified error-handling policy of any major conversational AI platform.*

::: {.callout}
Google's public conversation design documentation specifies exact limits: no more than three No Input or No Match errors in a row, and no more than two collection attempts for a single piece of information, before the system must change strategy.
:::

**The design lesson:** publishing exact numeric thresholds makes Google's platform unusually testable — a designer can verify a build actually complies, not just "feels okay."

## Case Study · An Enterprise Chatbot (Fictitious Inc.)

*Freed's own extended example — the design process behind a real retail deployment.*

::: {.callout}
Fictitious Inc.'s dream team prioritized store hours and locations first — high volume, low complexity — then layered in appointment scheduling and password resets in a second milestone.
:::

- **Cross-cutting concerns shaped the roadmap** — authentication, CRM logging, and legal review for the Report Fraud intent all had to be designed in, not bolted on
- **Change management kept the team in sync** — a single-editor checkout process for the process-flow diagrams prevented merge chaos

## Comparing the Three: What Each Gets Right {background-color="#BA0C2F"}

*Different platforms, different constraints — but the same underlying patterns.*

| | Focus | What it teaches |
|---|---|---|
| **Alexa** | Designing for the detour | A voice-first ecosystem where handling off-script users gracefully defines quality |
| **Google Assistant** | Precise, testable thresholds | Numeric limits make good design verifiable, not just felt |
| **Enterprise chatbot** | Process discipline at scale | Prioritization and change management keep a multidisciplinary team aligned |

## Connecting Back: Patterns Meet Principles {background-color="#F19C49"}

*Every pattern in Part 2 traces back to the same underlying idea: technology should adapt to people.*

| Pattern | Principle | Why they connect |
|---|---|---|
| **Happy path + fallback** | Weiser's calm technology | A design that only works on the happy path forces users to adapt to the machine |
| **Clarification loops** | "Assume cooperation" | Google's principle is a practical descendant of designing for how people think |
| **Graceful degradation** | WCAG's Robust principle | A system that keeps working, in some form, as conditions change |

## Discussion Questions {background-color="#003B5C" .smaller}

*Bring your answers to at least one of these to class.*

1. Think of a real conversational AI interaction where you left the happy path. Did the system handle it like Amazon's "good example," or like the rigid one?
2. Google publishes exact numeric thresholds (3 errors, 2 collection attempts). What would the right thresholds be for your own course project's assistant, and why?
3. Apply Weiser's "calm technology" framing to an AI assistant you use daily. Does it feel like it disappears into your life, or does it constantly remind you it's a machine?
4. Pick one WCAG principle and design one concrete dialogue-management rule for a voice assistant that would satisfy it.

## Key Takeaways

*Good design isn't a feeling — it's a set of testable, repeatable patterns.*

- Effective process design starts with prioritizing by volume and complexity, and it takes a multidisciplinary team, not just a developer, to do it well.
- Four dialogue management patterns recur across every serious conversational AI platform: happy paths, fallbacks, clarification loops, and graceful degradation.
- The best-documented platforms turn these patterns into precise rules — Google's 2–3 error thresholds and Freed's two-strikes rule reflect user patience as a finite, designable resource.
- Good conversational design and accessibility are the same underlying discipline, applied to different constraints.
